events.title: Danish colonisation and trade monopoly
hints: A Lutheran missionary landed in 1721 and the Crown later declared a monopoly over trade.
A state trading department fixed prices and controlled access to the Arctic hunting society.
The colony was made an integral part of the realm in 1953.
events.summary: The missionary Hans Egede founded a settlement in 1721, and Denmark-Norway later claimed the whole coast. A royal trading department held the monopoly on trade from 1776 into the 20th century. In 1953 the colonial status was ended and the island became an integral part of Denmark.

events.title: Ivittuut cryolite mine
hints: A mine on the southwest coast became the world's main source of a mineral used in aluminium smelting.
During the Second World War it supplied the Allies after Denmark was occupied.
It closed in 1987 after more than a century of operation.
events.summary: The cryolite deposit at Ivittuut was the world's main source of the mineral, essential to aluminium smelting. Danish engineers began mining it in 1859 and a Danish company held a monopoly from 1864. The mine's strategic value drew a US military presence in the Second World War, and it closed in 1987.

events.title: Thule Air Base and the relocation of the Inughuit
hints: In the early Cold War a huge military base was built at the edge of the northernmost settlement.
About 100 Inughuit were given four days' notice to move in 1953.
The hunters were resettled far from their traditional grounds, and in 1999 a court awarded compensation.
events.summary: The United States built Thule Air Base from 1951 under a defence agreement with Denmark. In 1953 the roughly 100 Inughuit living at Uummannaq were relocated about 100 km north. Danish courts later awarded them compensation, in 1999 and 2003.

events.title: Little Danes experiment
hints: In 1951 a Nordic government took a group of young children from their families to be educated abroad.
The aim was to raise a cultural elite that would be fluent in the colonial power's language.
Many were later placed in a children's home, and an official apology came in 2022.
events.summary: In 1951 Denmark sent 22 Greenlandic children to Denmark to be educated as a Danish-speaking elite. Many were placed in a children's home, and many lost contact with their families. Denmark's prime minister apologised to the surviving participants in 2022.

events.title: Norse settlements
hints: An Icelandic outlaw exiled for killing a man explored an ice-covered land in 982 and gave it a deliberately cheerful name.
About 700 settlers in a fleet of ships followed in 986 and founded farming colonies in the south-west.
The last written record of the colonies is a wedding in 1408, and they were gone by the mid-15th century.
events.summary: After Erik the Red explored the coast in 982, settlers from Iceland founded the Eastern and Western Settlements from 986, and the colonies exported goods such as walrus ivory and furs to Europe. The Thule people, ancestors of modern Inuit, arrived from about 1200 and were dominant by 1300. The last written record of the Norse is a wedding in 1408, and the Eastern Settlement had disappeared by the mid-15th century.
events.quip: Erik the Red's marketing deserves credit: nothing about the place was especially green.
